claim: IRS Publication 334 is labeled for use in preparing 2025 returns.
evidence: For use in preparing 2025 Returns

claim: When the production, purchase, or sale of merchandise is an income-producing factor in your business, you must generally take inventories into account.
evidence: When the production, purchase, or sale of merchandise is an income-producing factor in your business, you must generally take inventories into account.

claim: Publication 334 says you qualify as a small business taxpayer if you have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation).
evidence: have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation)

claim: The 2025 Schedule C instructions use the same test: average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation).
evidence: have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation)

claim: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory.
evidence: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory.

claim: A small business taxpayer that does not keep an inventory can treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or use a method that conforms to its financial accounting treatment of inventories.
evidence: conforms to your financial accounting treatment of inventories

claim: Under the non-incidental materials and supplies treatment, you deduct the cost of inventoriable items in the year in which they are first used or consumed in your operations.
evidence: in the year in which they are first used or consumed in your operations

claim: If you make or buy goods to sell, you can deduct the cost of goods sold from your gross receipts on Schedule C (Form 1040).
evidence: If you make or buy goods to sell, you can deduct the cost of goods sold from your gross receipts on Schedule C (Form 1040).

claim: Schedule C line 35 is inventory at beginning of year; if it differs from last year's closing inventory, you attach an explanation.
evidence: Inventory at beginning of year. If different from last year's closing inventory, attach explanation.

claim: Line 36 is purchases less the cost of items withdrawn for personal use, and the cost of withdrawn items must be excluded from merchandise bought for sale.
evidence: you must exclude this cost from the total amount of merchandise you bought for sale

claim: Line 37 is cost of labor, and you do not include any amounts paid to yourself; Pub 334 adds that labor costs are usually an element of cost of goods sold only in a manufacturing or mining business.
evidence: Labor costs are usually an element of cost of goods sold only in a manufacturing or mining business.
verifier_note: Corrected: added Pub 334's manufacturing/mining qualifier so the page's 'lines 37 and 38 are framed around manufacturing' sentence is supported; table row reworded to match.

claim: Materials and supplies, such as hardware and chemicals, used in manufacturing goods are charged to cost of goods sold (line 38).
evidence: Materials and supplies, such as hardware and chemicals, used in manufacturing goods are charged to cost of goods sold.

claim: Line 39 other costs include containers and packages that are an integral part of the product manufactured; freight-in, express-in, and cartage-in on raw materials, supplies you use in production, and merchandise purchased for sale; and overhead expenses such as rent, heat, light, power, insurance and depreciation.
evidence: Freight-in, express-in, and cartage-in on raw materials, supplies you use in production, and merchandise purchased for sale
verifier_note: Corrected: drafted claim cut the freight-in sentence off at 'raw materials'; Pub 334 (2025) ch. 6 line 39 continues 'supplies you use in production, and merchandise purchased for sale'. Containers sentence is 'Containers and packages that are an integral part of the product manufactured are a part of your cost of goods sold'; insurance confirmed in overhead list. Page sentence on containers softened from 'only when' (not stated) to 'when'.

claim: The total of lines 35 through 39 equals the cost of the goods available for sale during the year (line 40).
evidence: The total of lines 35 through 39 equals the cost of the goods available for sale during the year.

claim: Closing inventory on line 41 will usually become the beginning inventory of your next tax year.
evidence: will usually become the beginning inventory of your next tax year

claim: Line 42, cost of goods sold, is line 40 minus line 41, and the result is entered on line 4 of Schedule C.
evidence: Cost of goods sold. Subtract line 41 from line 40. Enter the result here and on line 4.

claim: Returns and allowances include cash or credit refunds you make to customers, rebates, and other allowances.
evidence: Returns and allowances include cash or credit refunds you make to customers, rebates, and other allowances.

claim: Sales returns and allowances are reported as a positive number on Schedule C line 2.
evidence: Report your sales returns and allowances as a positive number on line 2.

claim: Schedule C line 1 is gross receipts from your trade or business, and you should check any Forms 1099 you received for business income that must be reported on it.
evidence: Be sure to check any Forms 1099 you received for business income that must be reported on this line.

claim: Gross profit is figured by subtracting cost of goods sold (line 4) from net receipts (line 3).
evidence: Next, subtract the cost of goods sold (line 4) from net receipts (line 3).

claim: If you collect state and local sales taxes imposed on you as the seller, you must include the amount collected in gross receipts.
evidence: you must include the amount collected in gross receipts

claim: Trade discounts are the differences between the stated prices of articles and the actual prices you pay for them.
evidence: The differences between the stated prices of articles and the actual prices you pay for them are called trade discounts.

claim: Your inventory method must conform to generally accepted accounting principles for similar businesses and must clearly reflect income.
evidence: must conform to generally accepted accounting principles for similar businesses and must clearly reflect income

claim: Inventories can be valued at cost, the lower of cost or market, or any other method approved by the IRS (Schedule C line 33).
evidence: Your inventories can be valued at cost, the lower of cost or market, or any other method approved by the IRS.

claim: Use the specific identification method when you can identify and match the actual cost to the items in inventory.
evidence: Use the specific identification method when you can identify and match the actual cost to the items in inventory.

claim: The FIFO (first-in first-out) method assumes the items you purchased or produced first are the first items you sold, consumed, or otherwise disposed of.
evidence: The FIFO (first-in first-out) method assumes the items you purchased or produced first

claim: The LIFO (last-in first-out) method assumes the items of inventory you purchased or produced last are the first items you sold, consumed, or otherwise disposed of.
evidence: The LIFO (last-in first-out) method assumes the items of inventory you purchased or produced last

claim: The cost of merchandise you buy is the invoice price minus appropriate discounts plus transportation or other charges incurred in acquiring the goods.
evidence: invoice price minus appropriate discounts plus transportation or other charges incurred in acquiring the goods

claim: Inventory includes purchased merchandise if title has passed to you, even if the merchandise is in transit, and goods out on consignment.
evidence: Purchased merchandise if title has passed to you, even if the merchandise is in transit

claim: Subnormal goods (goods you cannot sell at normal prices) should be valued at their bona fide selling price minus direct cost of disposition, no matter which method you use.
evidence: You should value these goods at their bona fide selling price minus direct cost of disposition, no matter which method you use

claim: Publication 538 is revised January 2022 and states the small business taxpayer test as average annual gross receipts of $26 million or less (indexed for inflation).
evidence: Have average annual gross receipts of $26 million or less (indexed for inflation) for the 3 prior tax years.

claim: Cash discounts are amounts your suppliers let you deduct from your purchase invoices for prompt payments.
evidence: Cash discounts are amounts your suppliers let you deduct from your purchase invoices for prompt payments.
